segments.text: A Mars probe was lost to a units mix-up.

image.file: File:Mars Climate Orbiter - artist depiction - climate-orbiter-browse.jpg

segments.text: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter launched in December 1998.

image.file: File:Delta II launches with Mars Climate Orbiter.jpg

segments.text: On the way, small thruster firings kept nudging its path.
Ground software from the spacecraft's contractor logged each push in pound-force seconds.
The specification required newton-seconds. Navigators assumed that's what they got.
Every push looked four point four five times weaker than it was.
It was aimed at two hundred twenty-six kilometres above Mars.

visual.label: Planned vs actual approach (diagram based on NASA's 1999 report)

segments.text: It came in at about fifty-seven. Eighty was the survivable minimum.

visual.title: CLOSEST APPROACH
visual.evidence: NASA MCO Mishap Investigation Board, Phase I report

segments.text: In September 1999, it slipped behind Mars and was never heard from again.
NASA's verdict: the mistake was simple. The checks that should have caught it failed.

image.file: File:Mars Climate Orbiter - artist depiction - climate-orbiter-browse.jpg

title: A Mars probe was lost to a units mix-up: pound-force vs newtons #engineering
description: In 1999, ground software from the spacecraft's contractor reported thruster data in pound-force seconds instead of the newton-seconds the interface specification required. Mars Climate Orbiter came in far too low, and NASA said the real failure was that its checks never caught the error.
sources: NASA, Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board, Phase I Report (10 November 1999): https://llis.nasa.gov/llis_lib/pdf/1009464main1_0641-mr.pdf
NASA/JPL, "Mars Climate Orbiter Team Finds Likely Cause of Loss" (30 September 1999): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/mars-climate-orbiter-team-finds-likely-cause-of-loss/
